text.en: Raju drew with a graphite pencil and looked at a picture of a diamond. His teacher pointed out that both contain carbon arranged in different ways.

Carbon occurs in elements and compounds found in living things, air, rocks and fuels. Many carbon compounds are organic, while carbon dioxide and carbonates are familiar inorganic examples. It has special features. Catenation is the ability of carbon atoms to join in long chains and rings, and tetravalency means carbon has four bonds. Carbon can form single, double and triple bonds, which is why there are so many carbon compounds.
Isomerism is the phenomenon in which the same molecular formula has different structural arrangements, and such compounds are isomers; C2H6O is an example. Allotropy is the existence of an element in different structural forms. Diamond, graphite and fullerenes are carbon allotropes. Charcoal and coke contain less ordered carbon structures and other substances.
Many plastics contain polymers with long chains of repeating units. Carbon is part of the backbone of many such polymers. Plastics can be useful and durable. Discarded plastics can persist or break into smaller fragments, and their environmental effects depend on the material and how it is used and managed. Unnecessary single-use items can add to plastic waste. Reduction, suitable reuse and local collection can help manage it.

text.en: Look at carbon in three settings: graphite in a pencil, carbon dioxide in air and sugars in food. These contain the same element in different arrangements or compounds.

board.text: Element carbon appears in several forms and compounds

text.en: Organic chemistry includes most carbon compounds such as sugars and hydrocarbons. Some common substances containing carbon, including carbon dioxide and calcium carbonate, are classed as inorganic.

board.text: Organic example: glucose · inorganic example: CaCO₃

text.en: A carbon atom can form bonds with other carbon atoms. Repeating that connection builds chains, branches or rings. This ability to bond to atoms of the same element is catenation.

board.text: Catenation builds carbon skeletons

text.en: In methane, carbon shares an electron pair with each of four hydrogen atoms. This simple example shows carbon’s usual valency of four.

board.text: Methane: C bonded to four H atoms

text.en: A structural drawing uses one line for a single bond. A double bond counts as two shared pairs and a triple bond counts as three.

board.text: Single, double and triple bonds show shared pairs

text.en: Ethane, ethene and ethyne each have two carbon atoms. They differ in the bond connecting the carbon atoms and in the number of attached hydrogen atoms.

board.text: C₂H₆ single · C₂H₄ double · C₂H₂ triple

text.en: A hydrocarbon contains just carbon and hydrogen. In a simple saturated hydrocarbon, carbon atoms use single bonds with one another. Unsaturated examples can contain double or triple bonds.

board.text: Saturated: only single carbon–carbon bonds

text.en: A molecular formula tells us how many atoms of each element are present. A structural formula adds information about the bonds. Compare connections when you need to identify a particular molecule.

board.text: Formula counts atoms · structure shows connections

text.en: Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same counts of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. In ethanol the two carbon atoms are directly joined. In dimethyl ether, oxygen separates the carbon groups.

board.text: Ethanol and dimethyl ether are structural isomers

text.en: In diamond, each carbon atom bonds to four neighbours in a network. This connected structure helps explain its hardness.

board.text: Diamond: four neighbours in a 3D network

text.en: In graphite, each carbon bonds strongly to three others within a layer. Layers can slide relative to each other. Some electrons can move along a layer, which helps graphite conduct electricity.

board.text: Graphite: stacked layers with mobile electrons along layers

text.en: Pencil cores use graphite mixed with other substances. Diamond and graphite illustrate allotropy because both are carbon arranged in different structures.

board.text: Same element · different bonding arrangement

text.en: A fullerene can have carbon atoms linked into a hollow cage. Carbon sixty is one example. Compare its separate cages with diamond’s continuous network.

board.text: C₆₀: a molecular cage

text.en: Charcoal and coke are carbon-rich materials. Their structure can be much less regular than a perfect diamond crystal, and real samples may contain other substances.

board.text: Carbon-rich materials vary in structure and purity

text.en: Many simple molecular carbon compounds have relatively low melting points compared with diamond. A strong network and separate molecules respond differently when heated.

board.text: Structure can affect melting behaviour

text.en: When carbon burns with sufficient oxygen, carbon dioxide can form. With limited oxygen, some carbon may form carbon monoxide. We compare these only in symbolic reaction diagrams.

board.text: Products depend on conditions

text.en: Carbon dioxide can dissolve in water and contribute to a weakly acidic solution. Carbonate minerals, such as calcium carbonate, contain carbon in a different combination.

board.text: Carbon can occur in gases and minerals

text.en: Many materials around us contain organic carbon compounds. The cellulose in paper and the sugars in fruit are familiar examples with very different structures.

board.text: Paper contains cellulose · fruit can contain sugars

text.en: A polymer contains many connected repeating units. Polyethylene is a common example. Long chains can have different properties from the smaller units considered on their own.

board.text: Polymer: repeating units along long chains

text.en: A resin code can identify the type of plastic used in an item. It does not guarantee that a local facility accepts that item for recycling.

board.text: A resin code identifies material type

text.en: A durable container can be used repeatedly when it is suitable for its purpose. Reducing unnecessary packaging and sorting waste according to local collection guidance can help limit discarded plastic.

board.text: Consider reduction, reuse and appropriate collection

text.en: For a final comparison, choose diamond and graphite or ethanol and dimethyl ether. Explain whether your pair illustrates allotropy or isomerism and name the structural difference.

board.text: Allotropy: one element · isomerism: shared molecular formula
